title.en: Giviok: The Voyage Past Whirlpool, Sea-Lice, and the Tail-Hag
title.zh: 吉維奧克：漩渦、海虱與斷尾老嫗之間

region.en: Open sea and other shore, Greenland voyage

texts.period: Inuit oral tradition; chiefly from a single manuscript, well known all over Greenland, English edition 1875 (Rink)

source.work: Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (Blackwood, 1875), tale 15 'Giviok', IA talestraditionso01rink

summary.en: Unable to abandon his motherless son, Giviok at last flees when the boy cries that his dead mother is walking outside with a stranger — the resurrected wife he then kills a second time and stacks in her stone grave. Paddling on, he cheats the whirlpool, feeds the sea-lice with gloves till his paddle-blades are sheathed, sleeps on a raft of sea-weed, and squeezes through two closing icebergs that bruise his stern. Warned by rowed-up human heads and a glittering tail, he foils the man-killing hag Usorsak with a flat stone on his chest — breaking her tail — kills her shrieking daughter, then wintered with two kindly halibut-haunting women whose bladders he fetches back through the tide. Coming home he finds his abandoned child a grown whale-hunter standing on a whale's back.
summary.zh: 吉維奧克不忍拋下喪母的幼子；直到孩子哭喊『死去的母親正與陌生人同行』，他二度殺妻，疊屍石墓，終於駕艇出走。途中他逃過漩渦，以手套餵飽海虱，睡於海藻浮筏，從合攏的冰山夾縫中擠過，艇尾被擠傷。借人頭堆與閃亮尾巴識破食人老嫗烏索薩克，以胸前置石使其斷尾斃命，再叉殺其女。後與兩位善良的大比目魚漁婦同住，為她們追回漂流的大魚。歸鄉之日，當年拋下的幼兒已是立於鯨背的偉大獵手。

sensitivity.note: Rink notes slight traces of the Hiawatha tale type. Killing of the resurrected wife and of the hag's daughter recorded as told in the 1875 source.

passages.text: Giviok, it is told, lost his wife and was about to leave his child and the place where she was buried, in despair. He only waited till the boy had gone to sleep, then let himself down from the ledge to the floor; but when the child began crying he again lay down beside him. Once he was all ready, stooping to get out of the entrance, but went back unable to leave his son. One day the little boy passionately entered the room, saying, 'My mother is walking outside with a stranger.' 'Thy mother is not here; she is lying under the big stones yonder.' 'Look for thyself, then' — and when Giviok did look out of the window, he actually saw his wife in the arms of another man. At this he got into a great rage, went out, killed them, and put them on top of each other into the stone grave. Father and son went to rest; but when the boy slept the father carried out his intention of taking flight, and passing through the doorway — this time resisting the cries of the boy — got into his kayak and hastened away.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 15 'Giviok'; not verbatim.

passages.text: He paddled on and on across the wild sea; he came to the whirlpool and was nearly drawn into it, but somehow escaped. Then he got among the villainous sea-lice: first he tried to keep them back by striking at them with his kayak-stick, but that was soon devoured; then he threw out his sealskin gloves, and seeing they lasted a little longer, covered his paddle-blades with a pair of old gloves, lest the beasts should attack his paddle before he could slip away — and managed to get past them. Continuing his voyage, he saw a long black line: sea-weed, so compact he got out and slept on it, then pushed himself and his kayak across with his hands. He paddled until he came in sight of two icebergs with a narrow passage between them, alternately opening and closing; paddling round outside them, they always kept ahead of him, so at length he ventured between — pushing on with great speed, he had just passed when the bergs closed together and the stern-point of his kayak got bruised between them. At last he caught a glimpse of something dark, and soon reached a great stretch of land looming ahead.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 15 'Giviok'; not verbatim.

passages.text: 'If this country be inhabited, I will be sure to find a bare rock' — and such a one he found, then a house by the smoking chimney. He went straight to it, upset the funnel, and hid; a female came rushing out — 'I wonder if any one upset it?' — put it to rights, perceiving Giviok, quickly re-entered, and as quickly returned: 'Thou art invited to step inside.' Inside lay a hideous old hag beneath a coverlet, who ordered her daughter to fetch berries; she returned with a great quantity profusely mixed with fat. 'They are really delicious,' remarked Giviok. 'No wonder; the fat is of quite a young fellow,' rejoined Usorsak, the name of the old hag — but Giviok answered, 'Fie! anything of that kind I cannot eat,' and stooping down noticed a lot of human heads all in a row beneath the ledge; and when the hag uncovered herself a little and turned her back towards him, he saw something glittering close behind her. When all were ready to go to rest, Giviok went outside and soon found a flat stone to cover his breast with, then lay down on the ledge beneath the window. No sooner did he seem to be sleeping than the daughter said, 'Now he is sound asleep,' and the old hag came jumping down from the main ledge — but on his feigning not to be quite asleep she cautiously returned; when he had become quiet, lying on his back with his breast exposed, the daughter said again, 'He surely sleeps now,' and the mother let herself down even quicker, jumping up where he lay and sitting down with all her weight upon his chest, crying out 'Oh dear!' — and instantly tumbled down. 'What a pity!' cried the daughter; 'Usorsak has broken her tail; she provided so nicely for all of us.' Giviok got up from his couch, let fall the stone, and escaped through the door, the daughter shouting after him, 'Thou rascal! wouldn't I like to have had a taste of thy fine cheeks!' — but he was already in his kayak, where he was nearly upset; rising again he broke out, 'Shouldn't I like to harpoon her!' and so saying killed her on the spot.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 15 'Giviok'; not verbatim.

passages.text: Continuing his journey he again reached a bare rock, landed, went up to a house, upset the chimney-funnel, and hid himself; when the woman emerged and re-entered, he heard them wondering at the chimney having been upset, there being no wind. Invited inside, he observed the walls covered all over with hunting-bladders, the inmates a mother and daughter. The mother spoke: 'It will soon be low-water; it is a bad job for us that we have no one to haul in our draught when we have harpooned and fixed the bladders to the fishes.' 'I have my kayak close by, and have just come from the bad women yonder, both of whom I have killed.' 'Then thanks to thee!... We, too, have had men in our house, but these monsters put all of them to death; but now thou hadst better stay here with us.' To-morrow there would be low-water: when he heard a roaring noise he must hasten back, for then the high tide set in. He was sound asleep when awakened by the roaring waters and saw the daughter glide through the house-passage; hastening down to the shore, he was only in time to finish off a few of the halibut lying high and dry on the beach when the rising waters rolled great waves over him, and he had a narrow escape to the coast. The harpooned fish, floating by their bladders, drove across to the opposite shore; Giviok fetched them back in his kayak, for which the women were very thankful, and he remained with them for some time. After a while the memory of his son haunted him — 'My poor little son! what a pitiful thing it was to hear him cry when I went away! Some day I must go and see him' — and travelling back past all the dangers, he reached the opposite country and heard people singing: a great many boats tugging a whale along, on which stood a vigorous man. He did not recognise him; but this was his son, and he had been catching the whale. The father left him a weeping child, and now beheld him a great hunter, standing on a whale's back.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 15 'Giviok'; not verbatim.

title.en: Tiggak: The Sorcerer Who Sang the Sea and Ate the Brains
title.zh: 提加克：唱海、食腦的巫師

region.en: Ice fields and the enemy country beyond the isthmus
region.zh: 冰原與地峽彼端的敵邦

texts.period: Inuit oral tradition; abstract from three varying Greenland copies, English edition 1875 (Rink)

source.work: Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (Blackwood, 1875), tale 16 'Tiggak', IA talestraditionso01rink

summary.en: The lazy sorcerer Tiggak shames his brothers-in-law by hauling in two seals through a snowstorm, then prophesies their storm from drifting sea-weed, sings his one song of ocean foam to land them on a driving iceberg, and sings water out of its centre. Taken to a giant-house where his brother-in-law is hoisted through the ceiling to be flensed alive, Tiggak feigns defeat to kill the wrestler, answers his own 'Haul away!' to flense the flensers, calls down his blood-stained amulet from the boat-pillars to avenge them all, then eats the served-up brains, hands, and feet of his victim with shut eyes and turns the dish on the hag — who goes raving mad and dies. Sliding into the sea as a bear, he leads the whole party home transformed, the snow-bunting boy flying between their ears.
summary.zh: 懶散的巫師提加克風雪中拖回兩頭海豹，令內兄弟們羞愧；又憑漂向岸邊的海藻預言風暴，以一首海沫之歌將眾人引上漂流的冰山，再唱出冰心湧泉解渴。在巨人屋中，眼看內兄被吊上天花板活剮，他詐敗反殺摔跤巨人，學其聲音喊『拉繩』、『割吧』，讓屋上剮人者自剮其主；再呼血染的護身符復仇，閉眼吃下被殺內兄的腦漿手足，把菜盤一翻——老嫗發狂而死。滑入海中化為熊，他領眾人化熊泅渡歸鄉；雪鳥化身的養子飛倦了，便歇在熊耳之間。

sensitivity.note: Rink abstracted three Greenland copies; Labrador traces of the same tale exist. Cannibalism and killing recorded as told in the 1875 source.

passages.text: Tiggak was a famous angakok and sorcerer who married a girl with a number of brothers, and after this grew neglectful of his duties and gave up hunting: when the brothers-in-law left home in the morning they could not persuade him to follow, and sometimes he even slept till the first of the kayakers returned, doing nothing but keep his wife company and dawdle the time away. This offended the other men. When one of the brothers ordered boiled briskets, he said to Tiggak as they were served up, 'Do eat some meat — that is easy work'; Tiggak took a considerable quantity and ate away without giving any answer. In midwinter a gale from the north set in; the brothers lived solely upon stored-up provisions until these came to an end, and one day, when they could not even go out in the kayak, Tiggak was missing. Towards evening they looked about for him in a terrible snow-drift, and late at night heard a call and saw him approaching, dragging two seals along with him. From that time he rose in their estimation; he now had the briskets served up and addressed the brothers: 'Now come and fall to; the meat is boiled and served up, and eating it is easy work.' They all ate, but nobody spoke; and all the winter he continued providing for the others, in summer letting his brothers-in-law undertake the task themselves.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 16 'Tiggak'; not verbatim.

passages.text: Subsequently Tiggak adopted a boy as his son. Once more it was winter, the sea covered with ice as far as the eye could see, and Tiggak the only one to roam about upon the ice, looking out for the haze and seeking the open holes where sea animals resort to breathe. One cloudless, windless day he turned to his adopted son: 'To-day thou mayst come with us and try thy hand at seal-catching.' At the remotest islets he made an opening in the ice to examine the waters beneath: 'I believe it will come to pass; the sea-weed seems to be drifting landwards: just look' — the current setting towards land was stronger than usual, and he said, 'We shall have a gale presently; let us make all haste for the shore.' Though they could hardly credit his words, the weather being so calm, they left their seals behind and followed him quickly; then the snow was seen foaming on the mountain-peaks, and when they had only reached the first row of islets the storm burst strong and fierce and broke up the ice. Tiggak took his son's hand, running and leaping across the clefts, until a very broad one near the land: all jumped over but the son, who kept running to and fro along the edge; Tiggak took pity and returned to him — and then they all drifted away seawards, the waves washing over the floe, and they grew silent with fear. 'It is said that Tiggak is learned in magic art, and we are drifting out to the wild sea.' 'I only know a short song treating of the ocean foam' — and at once he began singing; they saw an iceberg close in front of them, watched their chance against its driving up and down, and Tiggak jumped first and got sure footing, the others following. Drifting further out, one remarked they would perish of thirst unless Tiggak knew some charm: 'I only know this one little song to get water' — and a little spring bubbled forth from the centre of the iceberg, which he tasted first, permitting them to drink only then, so it could not change.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 16 'Tiggak'; not verbatim.

passages.text: Drifting a long time, they came in sight of an extensive country; Tiggak warned that whoever leaped ashore must not look towards the sea so long as any were behind, otherwise their place of refuge would break up and be annihilated. One by one they jumped ashore without looking round; when the last had safely landed, Tiggak turned and exclaimed, 'Behold our place of refuge!' — and lo, nothing remained of it but a heap of foam. Crossing an isthmus they came in sight of many houses and were invited into one, hanging their outer garments on the boat-pillars; during the meal a squint-eyed youth with a shaggy head appeared in the doorway: 'The strangers from the east are hereby invited to pay a visit.' The host said, 'Since he presses you so ardently, you will be obliged to go.' In the other house a disagreeable giant-like man sat on the main ledge, beside him a similar old woman gnawing at a big shoulder-bone; pulling forth a seal-skin and spreading it on the ground, the huge man exclaimed in a deep voice, 'Now come on for a wrestling-match!' The brothers whispered Tiggak to take the first turn — 'Not so; you go down first, then I'll follow' — the other guests were ordered away, and the old hag fastened the door with the shoulder-blade. One of the brothers hooked his arm into the giant's; unable to vanquish him, he was obliged to give in, the strong man catching hold of his lower parts, falling over him, and with a deep groan crushing him to death. A rope was let down through the ceiling, the dead man's body fastened and hoisted to the roof of the house, where a sound of knives was presently heard, and one cried out, 'Here is his eye; let it be kept for our master.' Tiggak thought, 'In this manner I shall soon lose all my brothers-in-law,' and whispered to him who was going to stand forward, 'Just let me take a turn with him!' Hooking arms, the giant took a pull in good earnest, nearly hauling Tiggak's arm across; pausing a minute, Tiggak feigned to have been overcome, then suddenly threw him down and leapt upon him, the brothers coming to his aid and putting him to death in the same way he had treated their brother.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 16 'Tiggak'; not verbatim.

passages.text: Imitating the voice of the other, Tiggak now called out, 'A rope, a rope!' which instantly appeared and was made fast round the giant's neck; 'Haul away!' — once more the sound of knives was heard, until one cried out, 'Are we not flensing our own master? We'll make them perish down below!' — and they commenced pouring water down upon them. No means of escape appearing, Tiggak remembered that his amulet was sewed up in the lining of his outer jacket, left on the boat-pillars on their arrival, and called out, 'Bring me my coat that lies outside; I want it for a shroud!' Contrary to his anticipations it was instantly thrown down; catching hold of it, he loosened his amulet from within the fur-lining, put it into his mouth, and after saying 'Revenge us!' took it out again. Voices outside cried, 'He is falling! — and he too! — and there is another one!' — and after a while the amulet returned, covered with blood. Well wiped and cleaned, the owner again threw it out and cried, 'All of them!'; the next time no sound was heard outside. Pushing forward from a corner of the ledge they found their way out, saw no person alive, and went back to the first house to their meal — but the silly-looking youth again appeared: 'I'll tell you what — Apiak is now doing her very worst: she is cooking the brains, hands, and feet of her son.' Tiggak could not understand him, until a brother explained: it was the brains, hands, and feet of the one killed up yonder, and his mother probably intended to regale him with a dish made of them. When asked to go he would perceive an oblong dish right in front of the entrance, filled with brains nicely served up; taking hold of it quickly, standing erect with his face turned towards her and his eyes shut, he must eat it all up — if with open eyes, he would go mad and die — then turn the dish upside down, put it back in its place, open his eyes, and sit down beside the lamp. She would turn her gaze upon him and he would remain unchanged; when she took the dish and turned it round, the contents would be all restored, and he should say, 'Now, please, eat something thyself, as I have done. While she is eating, with her looks turned upon thee, just see what becomes of her!' Tiggak walked up to the house of the old hag and acted exactly as he had been told; having eaten, the wicked old woman turned raving mad and died. 'I have killed the old hag, but they will go on in this manner if we stay here; so we had better leave the place altogether and make for our home again.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 16 'Tiggak'; not verbatim.

passages.text: At a snow-covered hill sloping to the water's side Tiggak asked each brother what amulet he had taken when he had to make his choice — all answered a small piece of bear-skin: 'That's all right; you will all do very well.' But the adopted son could only answer, 'I don't know indeed,' and pressed, confessed: 'When I was able to judge for myself, I got a snow-bunting for my amulet.' Tiggak became silent and shook his head; after a while he remarked, 'And yet it may do; thou must perch down on us.' He let himself slide down the hill right into the sea, disappeared, and reappeared in the shape of a bear, shaking the water from his ears: 'Now follow me all of you' — and they were all transformed into bears. When the son's turn came he had not the courage, but at last went gliding slowly down and grew a snow-bunting, as such able to fly; meanwhile all the others were swimming homewards, and when the little snow-bunting got tired he took a rest between their ears. They landed a little to the north of their old homestead; climbing up the shore, Tiggak shook himself well and his bear-skin glided off, the rest all doing the same — and when the son's turn came, he shook off the snow-bunting's skin, and thus all of them marched home, except the one who had been killed.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 16 'Tiggak'; not verbatim.
